title: Geometric Policy Iteration for Markov Decision Processes

problem.claim: The work investigates the geometric structure of value functions and value spaces in finite discounted Markov decision processes.

gap.claim: The value function polytope and its relationship to the classical linear programming formulation require further characterization to inform policy-iteration algorithms.

contributions.claim: Characterizes the boundary of the value function polytope using a hyperplane arrangement and shows that the value space is a union of finitely many cells of that arrangement.
Introduces Geometric Policy Iteration, which updates one state's policy by switching to an action mapped to the polytope boundary and immediately updating the value function.
Supports asynchronous state-value updates, providing greater flexibility for large state sets than traditional policy iteration.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors explicitly present Geometric Policy Iteration as a new algorithm for solving discounted MDPs.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report that GPI achieves the best known policy-iteration complexity bound, expressed as O(|𝓐|/(1−γ) log(1/(1−γ))).
The authors report empirical demonstrations of GPI on MDPs of various sizes.

narrative_sequence.summary: Geometric structure in MDP value functions motivates analysis of the value function polytope.
The value function polytope boundary and value space are characterized through a hyperplane arrangement and related to the classical linear programming polytope.
The geometric analysis motivates GPI, which changes one state's policy using a boundary-mapped action and immediately updates its value.
The update rule targets faster value improvement while retaining computational efficiency and permits asynchronous updates for large state sets.
The authors report a best-known complexity bound and empirical demonstrations across MDP sizes.

source_observation.claim: The algorithm selects policy changes using the boundary geometry of the value function polytope.

interpretation.claim: Geometric structure can guide more targeted policy updates than generic policy-improvement rules.

application.claim: When an optimization problem has a characterized feasible or value-space geometry, use that structure to design localized improvement steps.

exception.claim: The abstract does not establish when the geometric update is preferable beyond the reported efficiency and flexibility claims.

source_observation.claim: GPI allows asynchronous updates of state values for large state sets.

interpretation.claim: Asynchronous execution can improve flexibility when global synchronous updates are costly or restrictive.

application.claim: Consider asynchronous state-level updates when scaling iterative decision algorithms to large state spaces.

exception.claim: The abstract does not specify the consistency, scheduling, or convergence conditions for asynchronous updates.

unknowns: The abstract does not provide proof details for the stated complexity bound.
The abstract does not specify empirical datasets, baselines, metrics, or quantitative results.
The abstract does not state the precise hyperplane arrangement, cell construction, or implementation requirements.
